name: Globe and Mail cryptic crossword No 3,343

clue.text: Ensuring quality of porridge, fan cooked with love

indicators.note: Porridge is cooked by being stirred round the pan, and letters given a stir do not come out in the order they went in.

blocks.note: eleven letters of fodder
love is the tennis score of nothing, written as a round O

explanation.surface: A devoted fan lovingly cooks a pot of porridge and checks it is up to standard.
explanation.walkthrough: Love is the tennis nothing and hands over the O, without which the mixture is a letter short of twelve. Proofreading is quality control done with a pencil, which is what makes the definition fair.
explanation.definitionFit: Proofreading is the last check a text gets before printing, the job of making sure nothing substandard reaches the page.

clue.text: Bone fish, having removed skin, at end of bar

indicators.note: Skin is the outside layer, so taking it off a word strips away the letters at either end.
What is put at the end of something is written after it, so the stripped letters follow the other piece.

blocks.note: the British drinking house, the local on the corner, in its three-letter name
the word FISH with its outer F and H peeled off

explanation.surface: A skinned fish served on the bone at the far end of the bar.
explanation.walkthrough: Hunting through the fish names is the false trail: it is the word 'fish' itself that gets skinned. The pubis is the bone at the front of the pelvis, the one the pubic hair is named after.
explanation.definitionFit: The pubis is one of the three bones of the hip, so 'bone' is the flat anatomical category the answer belongs to.

clue.text: Bad group leading me and you away from university

indicators.note: Whoever is leading is out in front, so that piece is written ahead of the letters it leads.

blocks.note: milk or meat that has gone off is bad
a camp is a group ranged on one side of an argument
me and you together are us

explanation.surface: A bad crowd is leading the speaker and their companion away from the university.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bad' is milk gone off rather than a wicked crowd, and the camp is a faction rather than a field of tents. Off campus is where a student is once clear of the university's own grounds.
explanation.definitionFit: A campus is the grounds a university stands on, so being off it is being away from the place, and both phrases work the same way in a sentence.

clue.text: Treated growth formed around middle of toe straight away

indicators.note: Something treated has been worked on until it is no longer as it was, which is licence to work the letters into another order.
'Around' gathers the letter beside it into the pile with the others rather than leaving it standing apart.

blocks.note: twelve letters of fodder
the middle letter of TOE

explanation.surface: A growth on the middle of a toe, seen to by a doctor without delay.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Straight away' sits where the doctor's advice would end, which is exactly where you stop reading it as the definition. Thirteen letters from a clue this short is the sign that almost every word is fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: From the word go means right from the outset, the same sense 'straight away' carries when something happens with no delay at all.

clue.text: Drink and drug served up by mum — that’s puzzling

definitions.note: The answer is a noun and the definition a description of one; an enigma is precisely a thing that puzzles, so the clause after the dash stands in for it.

indicators.note: Food is served up at the table, but in a down clue what is served up travels back up the grid, so those letters are written in reverse.

blocks.note: gin is the drink and E the drug ecstasy; sent back up the column they read ENIG
ma is mum

explanation.surface: Mum serving a drink and a drug at the table, which takes some explaining.
explanation.walkthrough: Only the drink and the drug turn round; mum keeps her two letters the way they are printed. E for ecstasy and gin for any drink are both standbys worth knowing.
explanation.definitionFit: An enigma is something nobody can account for — a person or a situation that resists explanation — so the clause describes it exactly.

clue.text: Eldest’s in garb, having changed at this?

definitions.text: Eldest’s in garb, having changed at this?

indicators.note: Changing is what you do with clothes and what the letters do here: the ones named turn up in a different arrangement.

blocks.note: seven letters of fodder, the apostrophe counting for nothing
six more, from the clothes the eldest is standing in

explanation.surface: The oldest child is standing dressed up, having got changed somewhere.
explanation.walkthrough: Every word does two jobs: the sentence describes someone who has got changed, and its letters spell the thing they changed at. 'At this?' is the only signal that a piece of furniture is wanted.
explanation.definitionFit: Read straight, the clue is the eldest standing in new clothes, and a dressing table is the bedroom piece you sit at to get yourself ready.

clue.text: Egg container on the counter

indicators.note: To run counter to something is to run against it, so the word is taken against the direction it is written in.

blocks.note: a tin is a container, here turned round

explanation.surface: A box of eggs left out on the kitchen counter.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface offers a kitchen worktop, and 'counter' turns out to be the other sense, against the way the letters run. A nit is the egg a head louse glues to a hair.
explanation.definitionFit: A nit is the louse's egg, the thing combed out of school hair, so 'egg' is literal rather than a figure of speech.

clue.text: Dad’s to have a go at Danish?

blocks.note: pa is dad, and the clue's own 's comes along with him
to have a go at something is to try it

explanation.surface: Dad is going to take a shot at something Danish.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe-s does real work here: it is two letters of the answer, not a contraction to read past. On a café counter a Danish is the sweet flaky thing, which is the definition by example.
explanation.definitionFit: A Danish is one kind of pastry, so the question mark flags a definition naming the whole by a single example of it.

clue.text: Expert old Italian comic

blocks.note: a buff is the enthusiast who knows everything about a subject, as in a film buff
o is the standard abbreviation for old

explanation.surface: A veteran Italian comedian who really knows his trade.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Expert' points at the amateur enthusiast rather than the professional witness, which is the step to take. Buffo is opera's comic part, the bumbling bass of an opera buffa.
explanation.definitionFit: Buffo is simply the Italian for comic, used in English of the clownish role and the singer who takes it.

clue.text: Regularly observed aircrew duties before a drink

indicators.note: What is observed regularly is looked at at even intervals, so only every second letter is picked up.

blocks.note: every second letter of aircrewduties, beginning with the i
the clue's own a, taken as it stands

explanation.surface: Cabin crew routines that get checked at intervals, done before a drink.
explanation.walkthrough: The evens run across the word break and stop one short, and the clue's own 'a' finishes the job. 'Drink' at the end is the definition, not part of the crew's evening.
explanation.definitionFit: Iced tea is tea brewed and then chilled, taken cold from the fridge, so 'drink' is the plain category it sits in.

clue.text: Main witness caught

indicators.note: To catch what somebody says is to hear it, so the word beside it is wanted as the ear takes it rather than as it is spelt.

blocks.note: to witness something is to see it, and this is that word by ear

explanation.surface: The key witness in a trial has been caught.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Witness' is the verb, to see, not the person in the box, and 'caught' is doing the listening — the courtroom surface hides both. Three letters leave very little room to hide in.
explanation.definitionFit: Main is the poet's word for the open sea, surviving in 'the bounding main' and in the Spanish Main, and kept alive since chiefly by crosswords.

clue.text: Hours will be needed to complete this!

definitions.text: Hours will be needed to complete this!

blocks.note: the reading the surface pushes: a groan that the job in hand is a long one and will eat the whole afternoon
the reading the setter means: the hours are what goes in the boxes, and entering them is what completing it consists of

explanation.surface: Someone warning that the task in front of them is going to take all day.
explanation.walkthrough: The hours are not spent on the thing, they are written on it. British employers hand the form out weekly and pay against what is entered on it.
explanation.definitionFit: A timesheet is the form on which hours worked are recorded, so it stays unfinished until the hours are filled in.

clue.text: Male elf in cast with wife and kids?

indicators.note: To cast is to throw, and dice thrown land as they fall, so the letters come down in an order nobody chose.

blocks.note: nine letters of fodder, the small 'in' included

explanation.surface: A male elf appearing in the cast alongside a wife and children.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' is the easiest word to read as grammar and leave out, and without it the count is two letters short. 'Cast' reads as the company in a play while asking for a throw.
explanation.definitionFit: En famille is French borrowed whole for 'as a family', and a man with his wife and children is one instance of it — hence the question mark.

clue.text: Enough beer to entertain politician

indicators.note: To entertain someone is to have them in the house, so one word takes the other inside it.

blocks.note: ale is beer
an MP is a Member of Parliament, Britain's elected politician

explanation.surface: There is beer enough here to keep a visiting politician happy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Entertain' is the hosting sense, having a guest in, not amusing one. The politician is always MP in these puzzles, two letters that slide into almost anything.
explanation.definitionFit: Ample means more than sufficient, so it swaps straight in as the adjective before a noun: ample room, enough room.

clue.text: Losing heart, becoming confused doing arithmetic

indicators.note: The heart of a word is the letter at its centre, and losing it takes that one letter out of the middle.

blocks.note: to addle is to muddle, so becoming confused is addling

explanation.surface: A person losing their nerve and getting muddled over their sums.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Losing heart' reads as courage failing, which is the trap; it is an instruction to a word, not a state of mind. Addle is the verb behind an addled brain and an addled egg.
explanation.definitionFit: Adding is the first of the arithmetic operations, so the definition names the answer by the commonest kind of sum there is.

clue.text: Stylish Compton’s last half-century, after opener’s dismissal

indicators.note: The last of a name is the letter it ends with, and nothing else of it is wanted.
The opener is the one who goes in first, and a dismissal sends them off, so the leading letter is taken away.

blocks.note: the letter the name ends with; Denis Compton was England's great batsman of the 1940s and 50s
a half-century in cricket is fifty runs, and FIFTY here goes in without its F

explanation.surface: Compton's final fifty, compiled after the opening batsman was out.
explanation.walkthrough: Cricket runs through the whole surface: fifty runs make a half-century, and the opener is the batsman who goes in first — here the F at the front of the word.
explanation.definitionFit: Nifty means neat and smart — a nifty bit of footwork, a nifty little car — which is the stylish sense applied to deeds and things.

clue.text: Heard shower at home stop

indicators.note: 'Heard' asks for the word as the ear takes it, which leaves the spelling free to be the other one.

blocks.note: a shower is rain, and this is that sound given the horseman's spelling
someone at home is in

explanation.surface: Rain heard falling while you are indoors.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shower' is the weather rather than the bathroom fitting. Reins are the straps a rider pulls on, and reining in has spread from horses to budgets and tempers.
explanation.definitionFit: To rein in is to pull something up short, so it is the checking sense of 'stop' rather than bringing a thing to a dead halt.

clue.text: Rotten plate of food, criminal notes

indicators.note: A criminal is someone who will not go straight, and letters that will not go straight do not stay in the order printed.

blocks.note: a dish is a plate of food, a course as served
the five letters of NOTES rearranged

explanation.surface: A ruined plate of food, written up as the work of a criminal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rotten' is the moral sense, a rotten scoundrel, and the surface parks it against the food to keep that quiet. 'Criminal' looks like a description of the notes and is the instruction instead.
explanation.definitionFit: Rotten said of a person means corrupt — a rotten copper, rotten to the core — which is the same charge as dishonest.

clue.text: Shock Englishman in Australia, falling over

indicators.note: Anything that falls over ends up the wrong way round, so the letters are read back from the far end.

blocks.note: a Pom is what Australians call an Englishman, and the word goes over backwards

explanation.surface: An Englishman out in Australia taking a tumble.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shock' is hair rather than surprise, which is the whole misdirection of the clue. Pom, probably short for pomegranate rhyming on immigrant, has been Australian for a Briton for a century.
explanation.definitionFit: A shock of hair is a thick unruly mass of it, which is exactly what is meant by a mop of hair.

clue.text: Manipulation of fabric seen periodically in applied arts

indicators.note: What is seen periodically shows up at fixed intervals, so every second letter is taken and the rest are passed over.

blocks.note: every second letter of appliedarts, beginning with the second

explanation.surface: A way of handling cloth that crops up now and then in the applied arts.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters run straight across the gap between the two words, which is what makes the evens hard to spot. Pleats are the folds of a kilt, stitched at the waist and loose below.
explanation.definitionFit: A pleat is cloth doubled back on itself and pressed flat, so the phrase names the handling and the answer is both that fold and the making of it.

clue.text: American grandmother carrying little David around

indicators.note: To carry something is to have it about you, so one word holds the other inside itself.
Turning around leaves you facing the other way, so the letters beside it are written back to front.

blocks.note: nan is the British child's word for a grandmother
David in little is Dave, and he is turned round

explanation.surface: An American gran carrying a small boy called David about with her.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Little David' asks for the short form of the name, not a small child, which is the step most solvers miss. Nevada is the desert state of Las Vegas and Reno.
explanation.definitionFit: Nevada is a state of the USA, so one of its people is an American — the definition naming the whole country where the answer names one part.

clue.text: Vehicle stuck in Pennsylvania

indicators.note: Something stuck in a word is lodged inside it, so the letters sit there unbroken and in order.

blocks.note: the letters run consecutively inside pennsylVANia

explanation.surface: A delivery vehicle held up in traffic somewhere in Pennsylvania.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stuck in' reads as a jam on the interstate while telling you to look inside the word after it. A state name that long can hide a vehicle without anyone noticing.
explanation.definitionFit: A van is the box-bodied road vehicle goods are delivered in, so 'vehicle' is the flat category word for it.

clue.text: Beautiful woman in British magazine

blocks.note: b is the standard abbreviation for British
Elle is the fashion magazine

explanation.surface: A beautiful woman photographed in a British magazine.
explanation.walkthrough: Elle is the French-born fashion monthly sold the world over, and it is the crossword's default magazine. 'In' does nothing but join the two halves together.
explanation.definitionFit: A belle is the beauty of the occasion — the belle of the ball — the French feminine for beautiful taken into English as a noun.

clue.text: A new type of word to stick in public statement

blocks.note: the clue's own A, taken as it stands
n is the standard abbreviation for new
a noun is one of the types of word the parts of speech are divided into
to cement things is to stick them fast together

explanation.surface: A freshly coined word being worked into a public statement.
explanation.walkthrough: 'To stick' wants cement in its fixing-fast sense, not anything jammed. The small words pay their way too: the clue's own A, then the N that stands for new.
explanation.definitionFit: An announcement is something said out loud to everybody at once — a birth, a delay, a resignation — which is what makes it public rather than private.
